newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Guinness, GrandMet say LVMH plan too costly.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Guinness, GrandMet say LVMH plan too costly.

text.p: Britain's Guinness and GrandMet on Wednesday dismissed as too costly and complicated a three-way drinks merger proposal from their largest shareholder French luxury goods company LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton.

The proposal forms part of LVMH Chairman Bernard Arnault's attempt to block the planned 24 billion pound ($40.2 billion) mega-merger between GrandMet and Guinness, to create a group called GMG Brands, which threatens to sideline LVMH.

"What (Arnault) is proposing is a complicated and costly break-up of both GrandMet and Guinness in order to leverage LVMH into a dominant position in what would already be the world's leading spirits and wine company," said GrandMet Chairman George Bull and Guinness Chairman Tony Greener in a joint statement.
But both companies agreed to study in detail LVMH's proposal with its advisers.
"The debate here is not about merger versus demerger. It is about creating the most value for our shareholders and ensuring that such value is fairly shared," said both chairmen in the statement.

They said Arnault's proposal, submitted to both companies earlier on Wednesday, would give him "back door control without paying a premium, and it is hard to see how this could be in the interests of our other shareholders."
LVMH holds a 14.2 percent stake in Guinness and has built up a 6.4 percent holding in GrandMet since the merger plans were announced in May.
The French group proposed merging its Moet Hennessy cognac and champagnes business with the United Distillers (UD) division of Guinness and International Distillers & Vintners (IDV) of Grand Met.

Under the LVMH proposal, the new company, to be listed in Paris and London, would be a world leader with 19 of the 100 best known wines and spirits brands and boast sales of 7.4 billion pounds for the year 1995/96.
Moet Hennessy would bring Moet & Chandon and Pommeroy champagnes and Hennessy cognacs together with Johnny Walker, Dewar and J&B whisky brands as well as Smirnoff vodka and Baileys Cream.
If Arnault has his way, LVMH would take a stake of some 35 percent in the new grouping in exchange for its 66 percent stake in Moet Hennessy and its holdings in Guinness and GrandMet.
However, analysts in London's financial district said Arnault was asking too much for his inclusion in the deal.
"Our belief is that he (Bernard Arnault) is asking far too much here," said Mark Puleikis, an analyst at Merrill Lynch who calculated that a stake of no more than 27 percent would be acceptable.
Analysts calculate that the 66 percent stake in Moet Hennessy owned by LVMH and its 14.2 percent stake in Guinness and 6.4 percent holding in GrandMet are worth about five billion pounds.

The combined value of Guinness's spirits arm, United Distillers and GrandMet's equivalent IDV is some 12.4 billion pounds. Moet Hennessy is valued at 3.8 billion giving a value for the entire drinks group of 16.2 billion.
On that basis Arnault might be entitled to a 30 percent stake in the business, analysts said.
"He is asking too much, because if you look at the valuations involved, 35 percent is unacceptable," said Charles Winston an analyst at HSBC James Capel.

LVMH argues that including Moet Hennessy in the drinks group would produce added cost savings by a closer integration of existing joint ventures operated in several countries by Moet Hennessy and Guinness owned United Distillers.
It would also benefit from the inclusion of a wider range of brands in cognac and champagne and greater geographical reach especially in Asia, said LVMH.

The proposal also envisaged the demerger of GrandMet's hamburger chain Burger King and its U.S. based foods business Pillsbury and Guinness brewing. The company also argues that by creating separately listed companies for food, fast food and brewing its proposal will add greater value for shareholders.
Some analysts agree there are cases where separately listed, single product companies, like Coca-Cola for instance, benefit from a clearer focus amongst management and often a takeover bid premium.
"The market would like purer companies, partly because of the focus and the bid premium attached but in many cases its not practical," said Russell Duckworth, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Guinness shares closed 14-1/2 pence higher at 620-1/2p and GrandMet shares were up 15-1/2p at 621-1/2 pence while LVMH gained 3.1 percent to 1628 in Paris but was off the day's high of 1,637.

LVMH added that if its plan was adopted it would drop its legal action against the merger. LVMH had claimed that the merger plan constitutes a "control event" which allows it to buy back the 34 percent stake Guinness holds in Moet Hennessy at a discount and buy Guinness's interests in joint ventures that the two companies operate around the world.
"They set us a task to come up with a proposal which would deliver additional value. This we have now done," said a spokesman for LVMH in London.
($ = 0.596 British Pounds)
